action_criteria.label: CSF tap test with opening pressure
action_criteria.rationale: In established Alzheimer's disease the decision to shunt rests on whether removing CSF changes the gait; the tap measures that directly.

action_criteria.rationale: The Alzheimer diagnosis was clinical only; biomarkers from the same puncture confirm the copathology that sets the expected cognitive benefit of a shunt.

action_criteria.rationale: Repeating the TUG at 2 and 24 hours turns the CSF removal into a test of shunt responsiveness.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform large-volume lumbar puncture before MRI excludes mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus

Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not attribute the whole decline to progression of Alzheimer's disease without evaluating the enlarging ventricles
Do not withhold shunt referral solely because of Alzheimer's disease
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 19% in TUG at 24 hours, the supportive MRI (Evans index 0.37 and enlarging, callosal angle 86 degrees, mild DESH) and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]

Counsel the patient and family that shunting is expected to improve gait and continence more than cognition, that Alzheimer's disease continues to need its own treatment, and agree the goals of surgery with them before the operation
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery

avoided_actions.rationale: There are no episodes of altered awareness or fluctuation, so an EEG cannot inform the gait and bladder decline.
The falls are gait falls with freezing and retropulsion, not syncope; an ECG adds nothing.
No cardioembolic or syncopal question exists in this case.
MRI is available and compares the ventricles and hippocampi with the prior MRI better than CT.
Rhythm monitoring has no role without syncope or palpitations.
Amyloid or FDG PET does not change the shunt decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test; the CSF from the tap answers the Alzheimer question at no extra procedure.
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are.
A 6-month afebrile decline with normal CSF cells gives no reason for prion, inflammatory or infectious CSF assays.

accepted: Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus with concurrent Alzheimer's disease (NPH-AD copathology)

differential.diagnosis: Alzheimer's disease alone (without a hydrocephalus component)
differential.key_features: The A+T+ CSF profile and MTA 3 confirm Alzheimer's disease, but it does not explain the magnetic gait, the incontinence, ventricles enlarging from Evans 0.28 to 0.37 or the 19% tap response.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic small-vessel disease
differential.key_features: Fazekas 2 white matter change can contribute to gait slowing and may coexist, but it does not explain the rapid ventricular enlargement or the tap response.
Freezing overlaps, but tone is normal with no rigidity, tremor or bradykinesia, and the gait responded to CSF removal.

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Generalised volume loss is only mild while the Evans index rose from 0.28 to 0.37 with an acute callosal angle, tight convexity sulci and a tap response.

differential.diagnosis: Secondary communicating hydrocephalus (post-traumatic, post-haemorrhagic or post-meningitic)
differential.key_features: No head injury, haemorrhage or meningitis in the history, and no siderosis on SWI.

key_clinical_evidence: Probable iNPH needs a progressive gait disturbance over at least 3 to 6 months with cognitive or urinary symptoms and no antecedent event (Relkin 2005); a pre-existing Alzheimer diagnosis does not exclude it. Here gait and continence declined over 6 months after a stable first half-year.
The MRI shows the Evans index rising from 0.28 to 0.37 in 14 months with an acute callosal angle (86 degrees), a mild DESH pattern and a patent aqueduct, alongside MTA 3 hippocampal atrophy.

Opening pressure 16 cmH2O with normal CSF content; after 40 mL, TUG improved 12% at 2 hours and 19% at 24 hours with fewer freezing episodes. A 10% or greater TUG improvement is a commonly used positive criterion; tap-test sensitivity is 26% to 61% and PPV 73% to 100% [Marmarou_2005].
CSF Abeta42/40 reduced and p-tau181 raised (A+T+) confirm Alzheimer copathology, which lowers the expected cognitive benefit of shunting without excluding a gait benefit.
Management is neurosurgical referral for a programmable-valve shunt with counselling on mainly motor and continence benefit, continued donepezil and memantine, and falls prevention.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Enlarging ventricles, a magnetic gait with freezing and incontinence, and a positive tap response identify a treatable hydrocephalus component; Alzheimer copathology does not preclude a gait benefit from shunting.
red_herrings.data_point: Alzheimer's disease (diagnosed 14 months ago by geriatric psychiatry)
red_herrings.intended_effect: All cognitive and motor decline is attributed to Alzheimer's disease progression and the hydrocephalus is missed

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]

findings.location: corpus callosum, coronal plane through the posterior commissure

signal_characteristics.description: High-convexity and medial parietal sulci tight; Sylvian fissures mildly enlarged. DESH pattern present, less marked than typical.
Bilateral hippocampal atrophy, MTA score 3, out of proportion to mild generalised cortical volume loss; temporal horn enlargement in keeping with the hippocampal atrophy.
Periventricular caps and halo with early confluent deep white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities, Fazekas grade 2. No lacunes.
Aqueduct patent with a flow void; fourth ventricle normal in size. No obstructing lesion, mass or aqueductal stenosis.

metadata.difficulty_variant_description: Diagnostic-puzzle iNPH superimposed on clinically diagnosed Alzheimer's disease: enlarging ventricles, a modest tap response (19%) and an A+T+ CSF profile from the same puncture.

patient.history_present_illness: A 75-year-old retired architect was admitted for evaluation of a decline in gait and bladder control that his neurologist felt was disproportionate to his known Alzheimer's disease. He was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease 14 months ago by a geriatric psychiatrist on the basis of episodic memory impairment and a structural MRI at that time reported as showing 'mild generalized atrophy'. He was started on donepezil and later memantine. Over the first six months his cognitive decline was gradual and he remained mobile. In the past six months his gait has worsened steadily: he now shuffles with very short steps, has had six falls, needs a walker and cannot manage stairs. Urinary urgency began four months ago and has progressed to daily incontinence. His wife says 'this is not like his Alzheimer's; something new is happening', and his cognitive decline also seems to have accelerated. A repeat brain MRI obtained last month at an outside facility was reported as showing enlarged ventricles not seen on the scan 14 months ago; the images are not available. His neurologist referred him for evaluation of the gait and bladder decline. CSF biomarkers and amyloid PET were not obtained at the time of the Alzheimer's diagnosis.

neurological_exam.additional: Bilateral grasp reflexes present. Frontal release signs prominent. No nuchal rigidity.
neurological_exam.gait: Severely apraxic, wide-based gait with very short shuffling steps and prominent freezing at initiation and on turning. Walks only with a walker. Pull test: multiple steps of retropulsion, near fall.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert; oriented to place but not to date. Reduced insight. Mild anomia in conversation. Formal cognitive screening reported separately.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal tone. Full strength. No rigidity. No tremor.
